drone.d: Emerged around 1990 out of minimalism and modern composition: single notes or chords stretched to extreme length, floating on slow shifts in overtones and volume, with almost no beat.

dark-ambient.d: Appeared in the mid-1980s where ambient met industrial: low-end rumble, cathedral reverb and sampled horror spaces that sound like an abandoned cellar.

glitch.d: In the mid-1990s Oval and their circle treated CD skips, bursts and software errors as rhythmic material, cutting glitches into rhythmic collages that IDM later absorbed in bulk.

plunderphonics.d: John Oswald coined the term in 1985: sampling whole passages of existing records, shifting speed and overdubbing them into unlicensed collages that challenge copyright and originality.

hauntology.d: A British sound current around 2006: faded TV soundtracks, old tape noise and ghostly reverb collaged into the nostalgia and unease of a lost future; the Caretaker and Burial are its exemplars.

noise.d: Breaking away from industrial and experimental music in the mid-1970s: no melody or beat, only feedback, distortion and enormous volume, with sound itself treated as material.

illbient.d: DJ Spooky coined the term in New York in 1994: hip-hop sampling and dub low end soaked in ambience, with loose rhythms and damp spaces, like a block after the clubs empty at dawn.

chillwave.d: Rose with music blogs around 2009: cheap synths, tape hiss and heavy reverb making hazy pop songs like a summer afternoon, sweet in melody and deliberately smeared in production.

dungeon-synth.d: Named retroactively by fans around 2010: inspired by the keyboard interludes of early black metal, crude synths play medieval dungeon-like looping melodies, lo-fi and cold.

chiptune.d: From 1985, born of console and arcade sound chips: music built from square waves, triangle waves and noise channels, bright in melody and limited in timbre, later the sound of indie games.

juke.d: Took shape on Chicago's South Side around 1997: ghetto house pushed to 160 BPM, with dense hi-hats, shouted vocal samples and relentlessly repeating sections, built for dance battles.

footwork.d: Evolved out of juke around 2005: more broken beats and harsher syncopation, packing countless sample slices into 160 BPM to match lightning-fast footwork, and DJ Rashad took it worldwide.

hard-trance.d: Split off from trance and hard dance around 1993: faster tempos, harder kicks and acid leads, pushed to its peak by clubs in Germany and the Netherlands.

tech-trance.d: Emerging around 1998: it keeps trance's melodic build-ups but swaps in techno's cold, hard drum kits and industrial timbres, highly driving and made for big warehouse floors.

vocal-trance.d: Took shape around 1996: built around full songs sung by female vocalists, verses building into exploding choruses, lyrics mostly about love and parting; Above & Beyond took it mainstream.

dream-trance.d: Appeared in Italy around 1994: soft piano and strings, long female vocals and a steady four-on-the-floor kick, sounding like dreaming awake; Robert Miles made it a global hit.

eurodance.d: Appeared in Europe around 1989: rap verses plus female choruses, bright synth timbres and a punchy four-on-the-floor, with catchy hooks made for radio and commercial dancefloors.

eurobeat.d: Developed by Italian producers around 1987: fast 4/4, dense synths and shout-along vocals, which found fame mainly through Japanese records and arcade games.

uk-hardcore.d: UK breakbeat hardcore of 1991: hip-hop and house samples, piano stabs and ever-accelerating breaks mixed with rave shouts, the forerunner of jungle.

speedcore.d: Split off from gabber around 1994: tempos pushed past 250 BPM, kicks distorted into a wall of noise, melody almost gone, leaving only impact and extreme emotion.

breakcore.d: Took shape around 1994: drum & bass breaks cut to the point of losing control, layered with hardcore, anime samples and noise, chaotic in structure and dense with information, like a city on fast-forward.

ragga-jungle.d: Appeared in London around 1993: jungle breaks topped with reggae and dancehall DJ chat and Jamaican-accented samples, closely tied to dancefloor and soundsystem culture.

techstep.d: Split off from drum & bass around 1996: reggae vocals removed in favour of cinematic dark timbres, industrial drum kits and precise low end; Ed Rush and Optical set its template.

jump-up.d: Emerged around 1994: bouncy basslines and simple catchy melodies, blunt drums and repeating sections designed for instant dancefloor reaction, with DJ Zinc as a key figure.

brostep.d: Split from dubstep around 2009: wobble bass turned into harsh mid-range metallic noise, with exaggerated drums and half-time rhythms; Skrillex carried it onto the mainstream charts.

riddim.d: Split again from brostep around 2012: melody stripped out, leaving minimal triplet bass and repeating drum patterns, one loop polished over and over while the floor runs on low end.

halftime.d: Emerged around 2010: drum & bass at 170 BPM played to feel half-speed, with sparse drums and heavy bass, stretching the sense of speed and sitting between drum & bass and dubstep.

drumstep.d: Emerged around 2010: dubstep bass and timbres placed inside the 170 BPM drum & bass frame, half-speed drums with violent drops, a hybrid of the two dance styles.
